screens.title: Python's list, typed
screens.question: What does it print?

options.why: You counted from 1. Indices start at 0, as in Python, so `closes[1]` is the second close.
You took `size()` as the last index. It counts the elements: three.
`closes` starts empty, but each `push_back` adds one element and `size()` counts them.

hints.text: `size()` is Python's `len`.
Which element sits at index 1?
Three elements; `closes[1]` is the second, 102.0, which `std::cout` prints as 102.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the `push_back` calls, then index from 0.

explain.text: `push_back` is `append`, `size()` is `len` and `[]` indexes from 0. `std::cout` prints 102.0 as `102`. Unlike a Python list, every element must be a `double`.

screens.prose: A vector keeps its elements side by side in one block of memory. The block often has spare slots; greyed boxes are not part of it. Slide to push back closes one at a time and watch the block.
screens.question: When 5 closes are in the vector, how many slots does its block have?

hints.text: Slide to 5 and count every box, empty ones too.

feedback.correct: Five in use, room for eight.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide to 5 and count all the boxes, full and empty.

byKey.five: You counted the closes in use. The block also has empty slots waiting for the next pushes.
byKey.six: You assumed one spare slot. Watch what happens at 5: the block jumps from 4 to 8.
byKey.ten: You doubled the 5 closes. The block doubles its own size, 4 to 8, when it runs out.

explain.text: When the block is full, `push_back` gets a block twice as big, copies the closes across and frees the old one. So the room grows 1, 2, 4, 8. At 5 closes three slots wait empty.

screens.title: Size, capacity and reserve
screens.question: How many times does `ticks` move to a bigger block during the loop?

hints.text: Does the loop ever fill the 1,000 slots?
600 is below the capacity `reserve` asked for.
The block holds 1,000 from the start, and 600 pushes never fill it.

feedback.correct: No moves: the room was there from the start.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare 600 with the capacity after `reserve`.

byKey.ten: That is the count without `reserve`: the block would pass 1, 2, 4, up to 1,024. `reserve(1000)` made room first.
byKey.eleven: You counted every allocation without `reserve`. Here one allocation, made by `reserve`, is enough.
byKey.one: `reserve` itself allocates once, before the loop, with nothing to copy. The loop never moves the block.

explain.text: `reserve(1000)` allocated room for 1,000 before the first push, so 600 pushes never fill the block. Without it the block would move ten times, copying 1,023 elements in all. `reserve` changes capacity, never size: `ticks.size()` is still 0 straight after it.

screens.title: A moving average
screens.prose: A moving average of `n` closes gives one mean per window: `len(xs) - n + 1` of them. In Python: `[sum(xs[i:i + n]) / n for i in range(len(xs) - n + 1)]`. If `n` is below 1 or above the number of closes, return an empty vector.
screens.question: Write `moving_average(xs, n)`.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB), and the first compile takes 10 to 15 s; later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs 7 hidden tests that call moving_average; each mean is accepted within a relative 1e-9, and an empty answer must be empty.

hints.text: Loop over the windows: window `i` covers `xs[i]` to `xs[i + n - 1]`.
Test 4 has 3 closes and `n = 4`. What is `xs.size() - n + 1` when `size()` is unsigned?
Return early if `n < 1` or `n > xs.size()`. Otherwise, for each start `i` from 0 while `i + n <= xs.size()`, add `n` closes and push back the sum over `n`.

feedback.correct: One mean per full window, and nothing when no window fits.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-4: With 3 closes and `n = 4` no window fits, so the answer is empty. If the program stopped, `xs.size() - n + 1` wrapped: `size()` is unsigned, so check `n > xs.size()` first.
byKey.test-7: `n = 0` has no windows, and dividing by 0 gives nonsense. Return an empty vector when `n < 1`.
byKey.test-2: The second window is 102, 101, 105, so its mean is 102.67. Check where each window starts.
byKey.error: The program stopped. If the message says index out of bounds, a window ran past the last close: the last start is `xs.size() - n`.

explain.text: There are `xs.size() - n + 1` windows when `n` fits, and none otherwise. Check `n` before any `size()` arithmetic, because `size()` is unsigned and cannot go below 0. A running sum adds the newest close and drops the oldest, so each window costs one step.

screens.title: Reserve what you know
screens.prose: Simple returns $r_i = p_i / p_{i-1} - 1$: `n` closes give `n - 1` returns. You know that count before the loop, so `reserve` it and the vector never moves. One hidden test reads `capacity()` to check. Fewer than two closes give no returns.
screens.question: Write `returns_from(px)`, reserving the exact room first.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB), and the first compile takes 10 to 15 s; later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs 6 hidden tests that call returns_from; returns are accepted within a relative 1e-9, and test 5 expects capacity() to be exactly 5 for 6 closes.

hints.text: How many returns do `n` closes give?
Test 3 is empty. What is `px.size() - 1` then?
Return early when `px.size() < 2`. Then `out.reserve(px.size() - 1);` and loop `i` from 1, pushing `px[i] / px[i - 1] - 1`.

feedback.correct: Exact room, one allocation, no moves.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-3: An empty vector broke it. `px.size() - 1` wraps to a huge number, and `reserve` of that ends the program. Return early when there are fewer than two closes.
byKey.test-5: Six closes give five returns, so capacity should be 5. If you got 8, the vector grew by doubling: call `reserve(px.size() - 1)` before the loop.
byKey.test-1: 100 to 110 is a return of 0.1. Divide by the earlier close, `px[i - 1]`, then subtract 1.

explain.text: `reserve(px.size() - 1)` makes one allocation of the exact size, so `push_back` never copies. The early return matters: on an empty vector `px.size() - 1` wraps to about 18 quintillion. A vector built with `out(px.size() - 1)` and filled by index works too.

screens.title: begin and end
screens.question: What is `total` after the loop?

hints.text: Where does `it` start, and when does it stop?
`it` starts at index 1. It stops on reaching `end()`, which is past index 3.
Add the closes at indices 1, 2 and 3.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start at index 1 and stop after index 3.

byKey.all: You added index 0 too. `begin() + 1` starts one element in.
byKey.short: You stopped before index 3. `end()` is one past the last element, so index 3 is still read.
byKey.end: You read a fifth element at `end()`. `end()` marks the place after the last close and holds no value.

explain.text: `it` visits indices 1, 2 and 3; the loop stops when `it` equals `end()`. Because `end()` is one past the last, a range is `[begin, end)`, like Python's slices. The range-based `for (double p : px)` uses these same two iterators.

screens.title: The three largest
screens.prose: A program reads prices until the input ends. You do not know how many, so a vector fits. `std::sort(v.begin(), v.end())` from `<algorithm>` sorts ascending; lesson 16 says more. Print the three largest, largest first. With fewer than three, print them all.
screens.question: Complete the program.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB), and the first compile takes 10 to 15 s; later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs your program 6 times with different input on std::cin and compares what it prints.

hints.text: First keep every price with `push_back`, then sort.
After an ascending sort the largest sits at index `size() - 1`.
Sort, then print `prices[prices.size() - 1 - k]` for `k` from 0 while `k < 3 && k < prices.size()`.

feedback.correct: Collect, sort, print from the back.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-2: With two prices you must print just those two. Stop at `prices.size()` as well as at 3.
byKey.test-3: No input means no output. If the program stopped, it read `prices[size() - 1]` from an empty vector.
byKey.test-1: Largest first: 104, 102.25, 101.5. If you printed 99.8 first, you printed from the front of the ascending sort.
byKey.error: The program stopped. With fewer than three prices, a loop that always runs three times reads past the end.

explain.text: The `while (std::cin >> p)` loop stops when input runs out, and `push_back` grows the vector as needed. The print loop has two limits, 3 and `size()`, so short inputs are safe. The test `k < prices.size()` compares two unsigned values, so nothing wraps.

screens.title: Checked access
screens.prose: `px[i]` does no check of its own: past the end it reads whatever memory is there. `px.at(i)` checks and throws `std::out_of_range`. This app cannot catch exceptions, so a throw ends the program, which the hidden tests look for. A desk build could catch it.
screens.question: Change `price_change` so a bad day throws `std::out_of_range`.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB), and the first compile takes 10 to 15 s; later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs 5 hidden tests that call price_change. Tests 3 to 5 pass a day that does not exist and expect the program to end with std::out_of_range.

hints.text: Which member function checks the index?
Test 3 asks for day 3 of three closes.
`return px.at(to) - px.at(from);`

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-3: Day 3 does not exist. With `[]` this app's library stops the program with a crash, not `std::out_of_range`. Use `px.at(to)`.
byKey.test-4: Day −1 does not exist either. `at` converts it to a huge unsigned index and throws.
byKey.test-5: An empty vector has no day 0. `at` throws for it too.

explain.text: `at` compares the index with `size()` and throws `std::out_of_range` when it is too big. `[]` skips that check, so it is a little faster and undefined past the end. This app's library traps `[]` too, as a crash; a normal release build reads garbage.

screens.title: Erasing while you loop
screens.question: What does `ticks` hold after the loop, in this app's run?

options.why: You assumed the loop sees every element. After `erase`, the next zero slides into the erased place, and `++it` steps over it.
It compiles cleanly. The compiler cannot see that `it` is no longer valid.
Only `at` throws that. `erase` and `++it` do no checks of their own.

hints.text: Draw the vector after the first `erase`.
After erasing index 1, the second zero moves to index 1. Where does `++it` go next?
`it` moves on to index 2, which now holds 101.5. The zero at index 1 is never examined.

feedback.correct: One zero survives: `++it` stepped over it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Shift the elements left after each `erase` and follow `it`.

byKey.clean: You assumed every zero was seen. After `erase`, the second zero slides into index 1, and `++it` skips past it.

screens.prose:
What you used, in one place.

```cpp
std::vector<double> v;        // empty
std::vector<double> z(5);     // five zeros
v.push_back(x);               // append; may move the block
v.reserve(n);                 // capacity >= n, size unchanged
v[i]; v.at(i);                // unchecked, checked
for (double x : v)            // begin() to end()
it = v.erase(it);             // next valid iterator
v.data();                     // pointer to the first element
```
screens.question: `v` holds three closes. What does `for (std::size_t i = v.size() - 1; i >= 0; --i)` do?

options.text: It never stops on its own: `i >= 0` is always true, so it runs past the start

options.why: That works for `int i`. A `std::size_t` cannot be negative: 0 minus 1 wraps to about 18 quintillion, which is still `>= 0`.
It compiles. Some compilers warn that the comparison is always true.
The first test is `2 >= 0`, which is true, so the body runs.

hints.text: Can a `std::size_t` ever be below 0?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow `i` from 0 to the next `--i`.

explain.text: `--i` at 0 wraps `i` to the largest `std::size_t`, and `v[i]` then reads far past the end. Count down with `for (std::size_t i = v.size(); i-- > 0; )` or use `v.rbegin()` and `v.rend()`. An `int i` works too, but then `i < v.size()` compares signed with unsigned.

screens.title: A price lattice
screens.prose: A binomial pricer stores its tree of share prices as rows: a `std::vector<std::vector<double>>`. Row `i` has `i + 1` nodes; node `j` has gone down `j` times. Build the tree from `s0`, the up factor `u` and the down factor `d`. `cpp-pricing` prices options on it.
screens.question: Write `price_lattice(s0, u, d, steps)`.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB), and the first compile takes 10 to 15 s; later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs 6 hidden tests that call price_lattice; prices are accepted within a relative 1e-9.

hints.text: Start with the row `{s0}`, then build each row from the one before.
Each new row has one more node: the top node of the last row times `u`, then every node of the last row times `d`.
Push `{s0}`. For `i` from 1 to `steps`: `row.push_back(prev[0] * u)`, then `prev[j] * d` for each `j`, then `tree.push_back(row)`.

feedback.correct: Rows that grow by one, built from the row before.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-2: With 0 steps the tree is the one row `{s0}`.
byKey.test-4: Row 3 should read 195.3125, 125, 80, 51.2. Node `j` went down `j` times and up `3 - j` times.
byKey.test-6: The middle of row 50 has 25 ups and 25 downs: 1.25 × 0.8 = 1, so it is 100 again.

explain.text: Each row needs only the row before: the top node goes up once more, and every node can go down. Rows of different lengths are why a vector of vectors fits. A pricer that only rolls back from the last row can keep one vector of `steps + 1` prices instead.

ideas: `std::vector<T>` is a growing array of one type: `push_back` appends, `size()` counts, `[]` reads unchecked and `at()` reads checked.
Elements sit in one block whose capacity doubles when full; `reserve(n)` makes the room once, so a known count never moves the block.
Iterators mark places: `[begin(), end())` covers every element, and `erase` leaves the old iterator invalid, so use the one it returns.

formula.name: Growth by doubling
formula.note: So `push_back` costs a constant amount on average.

summary.trap: Erasing inside a loop and then `++it` skips the next element; write `it = v.erase(it)` and step only when you did not erase.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. What does `v(3)` put in the vector?

byKey.one: You read `v(3)` as `reserve(3)`. It makes three elements, each 0.0, and `push_back` adds a fourth.
byKey.three: `push_back` always appends after the existing elements, so the size goes from 3 to 4.

explain.text: `std::vector<double> v(3)` holds three zeros already, so `push_back` makes it 4. To make room without elements, call `v.reserve(3)`.

options.why: You counted from 1. Index 3 is the fourth element, and there are only three.
That is what `px[3]` might do in a normal build. `at` checks the index first.
`at` never makes up a value: it checks and throws.

feedback.correct: `at` checks, and nothing here catches the throw.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. How many elements are there, and what does `at` do with a bad index?

explain.text: Three elements have indices 0 to 2, so `at(3)` throws `std::out_of_range`. This app cannot catch exceptions, so the program ends; a desk build could catch it with `try` and `catch`.

quiz.prose: A C library prices a strip of cash flows with `double pv(const double* cf, std::size_t n)`. Your cash flows live in `std::vector<double> cf`.
quiz.question: Which call is right?

options.why: `&cf` is the address of the vector object, not of its elements. It does not even have the type `const double*`.
A vector does not convert to a pointer by itself; this does not compile.
Only `size()` elements hold cash flows. The slots past `size()` are spare room, not data.

feedback.correct: `data()` points at the first element, and the rest follow in memory.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which expression is a pointer to the first element?

explain.text: A vector's elements sit side by side, so `data()` and `size()` are all a C function needs. That is also why `&v[0]` works on a non-empty vector.

quiz.prose: A tick buffer reserves a day's capacity at 08:00, and a strategy sums the day's prices every second.
quiz.question: Why is a `std::vector` faster for this than a linked list such as `std::list`?

options.text: Its prices sit side by side, so each 64-byte cache line the CPU fetches brings eight of them
A vector uses fewer additions to sum the same prices
options.why: Both add the same prices once each. The difference is how fast the prices reach the CPU.

options.text: A vector keeps its elements sorted
options.why: Neither container sorts anything. A vector keeps the order you pushed.

options.text: Inserting in the middle of a vector is cheaper
options.why: It is the reverse: a middle insert shifts later elements in a vector. The sum is fast for another reason.

feedback.correct: Contiguous memory wins: the CPU reads ahead.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about where each element lives in memory.

explain.text: A list scatters nodes across the heap, so each step can miss the cache. A vector's prices arrive eight to a cache line, and the CPU fetches the next lines before you ask. With `reserve`, the buffer also never moves during the day.
